title: True Mastery Requires a Beginners Mind
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article opens with judo founder Jigoro Kano's request to be buried in his white beginner's belt, using it as a launching point for a broader argument that true mastery ultimately circles back to humility and curiosity rather than settled expertise. It draws on Abraham Maslow's concept of "second naivete," the idea that self-actualized people return to a childlike openness even after achieving peak performance. The piece frames this as a costly choice — masters must risk looking foolish and let go of the comfort of their accomplishments — but argues it is the only path to continued growth for those who genuinely pursue excellence.
points: Judo founder Jigoro Kano asked to be buried in his beginner's white belt as a final lesson about mastery.
Psychologist Abraham Maslow's concept of "second naivete" describes how peak performers return to childlike curiosity.
Masters must choose between resting on established accomplishment or approaching their field again as a novice.
Embracing a beginner's mind requires freedom from worry about others' judgment and comfort with looking foolish.
The article frames this willingness to remain naive as the defining, costly trait of those who reach true mastery.
quotes: Kano knew that death, like true mastery, makes everyone a novice all over again.
Maslow called this quality a “second naivete,” in reference to the fact that everyone is born naïve and returns to that state as they reach the highest level of psychological development.
Masters explore the fundamentals of high performance with extreme humility, believing that new insights arrive through naïve questions and inquiry.
It requires the “student” to free themselves of worry about external judgments and to operate openly without fear of being seen as a fool.
Rare are the leaders and performers willing to embrace the beginner’s mindset and admit to themselves and the world that they know very little.
